forks.actual: Quibi launched on phones only. Whitman said the team had weighed living-room apps and decided the use case was “7 in the morning ’til 7 at night while you were on the go.”[^2] AirPlay came on May 27, Chromecast was promised for June, and the television apps on October 20, the day before the shutdown announcement.[^10][^30] Casting switched off Turnstyle, the feature that distinguished the shows.[^11]
forks.whatif: With television apps in April, the shows would have been available where a locked-down audience was actually watching. Roku’s later experience is suggestive: Deadline reported that more Roku accounts streamed the former Quibi shows in their first weeks than Quibi accounts ever had.[^20] But those viewers paid nothing. Television access might have lifted trial sign-ups without answering whether anyone would pay $4.99.

forks.actual: The service had two paid tiers and no free one. It tested a free, advertising-supported version in Australia and New Zealand a couple of months before closing.[^11] It said it had sold $150 million of first-year advertising, and by June advertisers were asking to renegotiate because viewership was low.[^3][^7]
forks.whatif: A free tier at launch would have put the shows in front of the 5 million or more people who downloaded the app, and given advertisers the audience they had paid for.[^9] It is the model Roku applied to the same library.[^16] Whether advertising alone could have covered programming at up to $6 million an hour is doubtful; the plan’s $250 million of subscriber revenue would have had to come from somewhere.[^3][^5]

forks.actual: When the pandemic arrived, Katzenberg and Whitman considered postponing. They went ahead on April 6 because twelve months of advertising was locked in and more than six months of shows were finished.[^4]
forks.whatif: A launch in 2021, with commuting partly restored, would have tested the original idea under the conditions it was designed for. It would also have meant a year of fixed costs with no revenue, renegotiated advertising, and a launch after TikTok’s pandemic growth rather than during it. The founders’ own view was that the cause was “a combination of the two,” the idea and the timing.[^1]
